1	# Introduction to Rendering
2	
3	Terminal outputs have significant limitations: single font, single size, no graphics. But modern terminals provide many facilities like true colors, light/dark mode support, adaptive sizing, and more. Rich, helpful, and clear outputs are within reach.
4	
5	The development reality explains why such output remains rare. From a primitive syntax born in the 1970s to the scattered ecosystem support, it's been a major effort to craft great outputs—and logically, it rarely makes sense to invest that time.
6	
7	`standout-render` is designed to make crafting polished outputs a breeze by leveraging ideas, tools, and workflows from web applications—a domain in which rich interface authoring has evolved into the best model we've got. (But none of the JavaScript ecosystem chaos, rest assured.)
8	
9	In this guide, we'll explore what makes great outputs and how `standout-render` helps you get there.
10	
11	**See Also:**
12	
13	- [Styling System](../topics/styling-system.md) - themes, adaptive attributes, CSS syntax
14	- [Templating](../topics/templating.md) - MiniJinja, style tags, processing modes
15	- [Introduction to Tabular](intro-to-tabular.md) - column layouts and tables
16	
17	---
18	
19	## What Polished Output Entails
20	
21	If you're building your CLI in Rust, chances are it's not a throwaway grep-formatting script—if that were the case, nothing beats shells. More likely, your program deals with complex data, logic, and computation, and the full power of Rust matters. In the same way, clear, well-presented, and designed outputs improve your users' experience when parsing that information.
22	
23	Creating good results depends on discipline, consistency, and above all, experimentation—from exploring options to fine-tuning small details. Unlike code, good layout is experimental and takes many iterations: change, view result, change again, judge the new change, and so on.
24	
25	The classical setup for shell UIs is anything but conducive to this. All presentation is mixed with code, often with complicated logic, if not coupled to it. Additionally, from escape codes to whitespace handling to spreading visual information across many lines of code, it becomes hard to visualize and change things.
26	
27	The edit-code-compile-run cycle makes small tweaks take minutes. Sometimes a full hour for a minor change. In that scenario, it's no surprise that people don't bother.
28	
29	---
30	
31	## Our Example: A Report Generator
32	
33	We'll use a simple report generator to demonstrate the rendering layer. Here's our data:
34	
35	```rust
36	use serde::Serialize;
37	
38	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
39	#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]
40	pub enum Status { Pending, Done }
41	
42	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
43	pub struct Task {
44	    pub title: String,
45	    pub status: Status,
46	}
47	
48	#[derive(Serialize)]
49	pub struct Report {
50	    pub message: Option<String>,
51	    pub tasks: Vec<Task>,
52	}
53	```
54	
55	Our goal: transform this raw data into polished, readable output that adapts to the terminal, respects user preferences, and takes minutes to iterate on—not hours.
56	
57	---
58	
59	## The Separation Principle
60	
61	`standout-render` is designed around a strict separation of data and presentation. This isn't just architectural nicety—it unlocks a fundamentally better workflow.
62	
63	### Without Separation
64	
65	Here's the typical approach, tangling logic and output:
66	
67	```rust
68	fn print_report(tasks: &[Task]) {
69	    println!("\x1b[1;36mYour Tasks\x1b[0m");
70	    println!("──────────");
71	    for (i, task) in tasks.iter().enumerate() {
72	        let marker = if matches!(task.status, Status::Done) { "[x]" } else { "[ ]" };
73	        println!("{}. {} {}", i + 1, marker, task.title);
74	    }
75	    println!("\n{} tasks total", tasks.len());
76	}
77	```
78	
79	Problems:
80	
81	- Escape codes are cryptic and error-prone
82	- Changes require recompilation
83	- Logic and presentation are intertwined
84	- Testing is brittle
85	- No easy way to support multiple output formats
86	
87	### With Separation
88	
89	The same output, properly separated:
90	
91	```rust
92	use standout_render::{render, Theme};
93	use console::Style;
94	
95	// Data preparation (your logic layer)
96	let report = Report {
97	    message: Some(format!("{} tasks total", tasks.len())),
98	    tasks,
99	};
100	
101	// Theme definition (can be in a separate CSS/YAML file)
102	let theme = Theme::new()
103	    .add("title", Style::new().cyan().bold())
104	    .add("done", Style::new().green())
105	    .add("pending", Style::new().yellow())
106	    .add("muted", Style::new().dim());
107	
108	// Template (can be in a separate .jinja file)
109	let template = r#"
110	[title]Your Tasks[/title]
111	──────────
112	{% for task in tasks %}
113	[{{ task.status }}]{{ task.status }}[/{{ task.status }}]  {{ task.title }}
114	{% endfor %}
115	
116	{% if message %}[muted]{{ message }}[/muted]{% endif %}
117	"#;
118	
119	let output = render(template, &report, &theme)?;
120	print!("{}", output);
121	```
122	
123	`render` is the convenience wrapper. The contract is `render_request`: an owned `RenderRequest` carrying data, template, theme, format, color policy, and `TargetProperties`. Wrappers detect destination facts at their edge, build that request, and delegate. They keep their own names. Tests construct `TargetProperties` rather than installing detector overrides (those APIs are removed).
124	
125	The same render as an explicit request — destination facts on `TargetProperties`, no process detection:
126	
127	```rust
128	use std::collections::HashMap;
129	use serde_json::json;
130	use standout_render::{
131	    AmbiguousWidth, ColorMode, ColorPolicy, IconMode, OutputMode, RenderRequest,
132	    TargetProperties, TemplateRef, Theme, default_template_engine, render_request,
133	};
134	use console::Style;
135	
136	let theme = Theme::new().add("title", Style::new().cyan().bold());
137	let request = RenderRequest {
138	    data: json!({"name": "Tasks", "count": 42}),
139	    template: TemplateRef::Inline("[title]{{ name }}[/title]: {{ count }} items".into()),
140	    theme,
141	    format: OutputMode::Text,
142	    color_policy: ColorPolicy::Auto,
143	    target: TargetProperties {
144	        width: Some(80),
145	        stdout_is_terminal: true,
146	        stderr_is_terminal: true,
147	        stdout_color_capability: true,
148	        stderr_color_capability: true,
149	        color_scheme: ColorMode::Dark,
150	        icon_mode: IconMode::Classic,
151	        ambiguous_width: AmbiguousWidth::Narrow,
152	    },
153	    engine: default_template_engine(),
154	    registry: None,
155	    context_registry: None,
156	    csv_projection: None,
157	    extras: HashMap::new(),
158	    warnings: None,
159	};
160	let output = render_request(&request)?;
161	```
162	
163	Now:
164	
165	- Logic is testable without output concerns
166	- Presentation is declarative and readable
167	- Styles are centralized and named semantically
168	- Changes to appearance don't require recompilation (with file-based templates)
169	- The same request, with file-backed templates and context providers held fixed, produces the same bytes
170	
171	---
172	
173	## Quick Iteration and Workflow
174	
175	The separation principle enables a radically better workflow. Here's what `standout-render` provides:
176	
177	### 1. File-Based Flow
178	
179	Dedicated files for templates and styles:
180	
181	- Lower risk of breaking code—especially relevant for non-developer types like technical designers
182	- Simpler diffs and easier navigation
183	- Trivial to experiment with variations (duplicate files, swap names)
184	
185	**Directory structure:**
186	
187	```text
188	src/
189	├── main.rs
190	└── templates/
191	    └── report.jinja
192	styles/
193	└── default.css
194	```
195	
196	### 2. Hot Live Reload
197	
198	During development, you edit the template or styles and re-run. No compilation. No long turnaround.
199	
200	This changes the entire experience. You can make and verify small adjustments in seconds. You can extensively fine-tune output quickly, then polish the full app in a focused session. Time efficiency aside, the quick iterative cycles encourage caring about smaller details, consistency—the things you forgo when iteration is painful.
201	
202	(When released, files can be compiled into the binary using embedded macros, costing no performance or path-handling headaches in distribution.)
203	
204	See [File System Resources](../topics/file-system-resources.md) for details on how hot reload works.
205	
206	---
207	
208	## Best-of-Breed Specialized Formats
209	
210	### Templates: MiniJinja (Default)
211	
212	`standout-render` uses MiniJinja templates by default—a Rust implementation of Jinja2, a de facto standard for rich and powerful templating. The simple syntax and powerful features let you map template text to actual output much easier than `println!` spreads.
213	
214	> **Alternative engines available:** For simpler templates or smaller binaries, see [Template Engines](../topics/template-engines.md) for lightweight alternatives like `SimpleEngine`.
215	
216	```jinja
217	{% if message %}[accent]{{ message }}[/accent]{% endif %}
218	
219	{% for task in tasks %}
220	[{{ task.status }}]{{ task.status | upper }}[/{{ task.status }}]  {{ task.title }}
221	{% endfor %}
222	```
223	
224	Benefits:
225	
226	- Simple, readable syntax
227	- Powerful control flow (loops, conditionals, filters)
228	- **Partials support**: templates can include other templates, enabling reuse
229	- **Custom filters**: for complex presentation needs, write small bits of code and keep templates clean
230	
231	See [Templating](../topics/templating.md) for template filters and advanced usage.
232	
233	### Styles: CSS Themes
234	
235	The styling layer uses CSS files with the familiar syntax you already know, but with simpler semantics tailored for terminals:
236	
237	```css
238	.title {
239	    color: cyan;
240	    font-weight: bold;
241	}
242	
243	.done { color: green; }
244	.blocked { color: red; }
245	.pending { color: yellow; }
246	
247	/* Adaptive for light/dark mode */
248	@media (prefers-color-scheme: light) {
249	    .panel { color: black; }
250	}
251	
252	@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
253	    .panel { color: white; }
254	}
255	```
256	
257	Features:
258	
259	- **Adaptive attributes**: a style can render different values for light and dark modes
260	- **Theming support**: swap the entire visual appearance at once
261	- **True color**: RGB values for precise colors (`#ff6b35` or `[255, 107, 53]`)
262	- **Aliases**: semantic names resolve to visual styles (`commit-message: title`)
263	
264	See [Styling System](../topics/styling-system.md) for complete style options.
265	
266	### Theme-Relative Colors
267	
268	Standard color definitions (named colors, hex, 256-palette) are absolute — they look the same regardless of the user's terminal theme. This can clash with carefully chosen base16 palettes.
269	
270	`cube(r%, g%, b%)` colors solve this by specifying a position in a color cube whose corners are the theme's 8 base ANSI colors:
271	
272	```css
273	.warm-accent { color: cube(60%, 20%, 0%); }   /* 60% toward red, 20% toward green */
274	.cool-accent { color: cube(0%, 0%, 80%); }     /* 80% toward blue */
275	.neutral     { color: cube(50%, 50%, 50%); }   /* center of the cube */
276	```
277	
278	The same coordinate produces different RGB values depending on the active theme — a Gruvbox theme produces earthy tones, Catppuccin produces pastels, and Solarized produces muted variants. The designer's intent ("warm accent") is preserved across all themes.
279	
280	The interpolation happens in CIE LAB space, ensuring perceptually uniform gradients with no muddy midpoints.
281	
282	To attach a palette to a theme:
283	
284	```rust
285	use standout_render::Theme;
286	use standout_render::colorspace::{ThemePalette, Rgb};
287	
288	let palette = ThemePalette::new([
289	    Rgb(40, 40, 40),    Rgb(204, 36, 29),   Rgb(152, 151, 26),  Rgb(215, 153, 33),
290	    Rgb(69, 133, 136),  Rgb(177, 98, 134),  Rgb(104, 157, 106), Rgb(168, 153, 132),
291	]);
292	
293	let theme = Theme::from_yaml("...")?
294	    .with_palette(palette);
295	```
296	
297	---
298	
299	## Template Integration with Styling
300	
301	Styles are applied with BBCode-like syntax: `[style]content[/style]`. A familiar, simple, and accessible form.
302	
303	```jinja
304	[title]Your Tasks[/title]
305	{% for task in tasks %}
306	[{{ task.status }}]{{ task.title }}[/{{ task.status }}]
307	{% endfor %}
308	```
309	
310	Style tags:
311	
312	- Nest properly: `[outer][inner]text[/inner][/outer]`
313	- Can span multiple lines
314	- Can contain template logic: `[title]{% if x %}{{ x }}{% endif %}[/title]`
315	
316	### Output Modes: Rich, Plain, and Debug
317	
318	`standout-render` processes style tags differently based on the output mode:
319	
320	```rust
321	use standout_render::{render_with_output, OutputMode};
322	
323	// Rich terminal output (ANSI codes)
324	let rich = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term)?;
325	
326	// Plain text (strips style tags)
327	let plain = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Text)?;
328	
329	// Debug mode (keeps tags visible)
330	let debug = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::TermDebug)?;
331	```
332	
333	**Single template for rich and plain text.** The same template serves both—no duplication needed.
334	
335	```rust
336	// Auto-detect based on terminal capabilities
337	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Auto)?;
338	```
339	
340	In auto mode:
341	
342	- TTY with color support → rich output
343	- Pipe or redirect → plain text
344	
345	> **For standout framework users:** The framework's `--output` flag automatically sets the output mode. See the standout documentation for CLI integration.
346	
347	### Debug Mode
348	
349	Use `OutputMode::TermDebug` for debugging:
350	
351	```text
352	[title]Your Tasks[/title]
353	[pending]pending[/pending]  Implement auth
354	[done]done[/done]  Fix tests
355	```
356	
357	Style tags remain visible, making it easy to verify correct placement. Useful for testing and automation tools.
358	
359	---
360	
361	## Tabular Layout
362	
363	Many outputs are lists of things—log entries, servers, tasks. These benefit from vertically aligned layouts. Aligning fields seems simple at first, but when you factor in ANSI awareness, flexible size ranges, wrapping behavior, truncation, justification, and expanding cells, it becomes really hard.
364	
365	Tabular gives you a declarative API, both in Rust and in templates, that handles all of this:
366	
367	```jinja
368	{% set t = tabular([
369	    {"name": "index", "width": 4},
370	    {"name": "status", "width": 10},
371	    {"name": "title", "width": "fill"}
372	], separator="  ") %}
373	
374	{% for task in tasks %}
375	{{ t.row([loop.index, task.status | style_as(task.status), task.title]) }}
376	{% endfor %}
377	```
378	
379	Output adapts to terminal width:
380	
381	```text
382	1.    pending     Implement user authentication
383	2.    done        Review pull request #142
384	3.    pending     Update dependencies
385	```
386	
387	Features:
388	
389	- Fixed, range, fill, and fractional widths
390	- Truncation (start, middle, end) with custom ellipsis
391	- Word wrapping for long content
392	- Per-column styling
393	- Automatic field extraction from structs
394	
395	See [Introduction to Tabular](intro-to-tabular.md) for a comprehensive walkthrough.
396	
397	### Ambiguous character widths
398	
399	Unicode marks some characters, including `≈` and `Δ`, as East Asian
400	Ambiguous. Standout treats them as one column by default, preserving existing
401	layouts. Applications that target terminals where these glyphs occupy two
402	columns can select the policy explicitly:
403	
404	```rust
405	use standout_render::{AmbiguousWidth, Renderer, Theme};
406	
407	let renderer = Renderer::new(Theme::new())?
408	    .with_ambiguous_width(AmbiguousWidth::Wide);
409	```
410	
411	The selection flows through measurement, ANSI and style-tag-aware visible
412	width, padding, truncation, wrapping, tabular formatting, and MiniJinja width
413	filters. Standout makes no locale-based guess and promises no automatic
414	detection. The policy-aware helper variants, such as
415	`standout_render::tabular::display_width_with_policy`, are available when
416	formatting directly.
417	
418	---
419	
420	## Structured Output
421	
422	Beyond textual output, `standout-render` supports structured formats:
423	
424	```rust
425	use standout_render::{render_auto, OutputMode};
426	
427	// For Term/Text: renders template
428	// For Json/Yaml/etc: serializes data directly
429	let json_output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
430	let yaml_output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Yaml)?;
431	```
432	
433	**Structured output for free.** Because your data is `Serialize`-able, JSON/YAML outputs work automatically. Automation (tests, scripts, other programs) no longer needs to reverse-engineer data from formatted output.
434	
435	Same data types—different output format. This enables API-like behavior from CLI apps without writing separate code paths.
436	
437	---
438	
439	## Putting It All Together
440	
441	Here's a complete example:
442	
443	```rust
444	use standout_render::{render, Theme};
445	use console::Style;
446	use serde::Serialize;
447	
448	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
449	#[serde(rename_all = "lowercase")]
450	pub enum Status { Pending, Done }
451	
452	#[derive(Clone, Serialize)]
453	pub struct Task {
454	    pub title: String,
455	    pub status: Status,
456	}
457	
458	#[derive(Serialize)]
459	pub struct Report {
460	    pub message: Option<String>,
461	    pub tasks: Vec<Task>,
462	}
463	
464	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
465	    let theme = Theme::from_css(r#"
466	        .title { color: cyan; font-weight: bold; }
467	        .done { color: green; }
468	        .pending { color: yellow; }
469	        .muted { opacity: 0.5; }
470	    "#)?;
471	
472	    let tasks = vec![
473	        Task { title: "Implement user authentication".into(), status: Status::Pending },
474	        Task { title: "Review pull request #142".into(), status: Status::Done },
475	        Task { title: "Update dependencies".into(), status: Status::Pending },
476	    ];
477	
478	    let pending_count = tasks.iter()
479	        .filter(|t| matches!(t.status, Status::Pending))
480	        .count();
481	
482	    let report = Report {
483	        message: Some(format!("{} pending", pending_count)),
484	        tasks,
485	    };
486	
487	    let template = r#"
488	[title]My Tasks[/title]
489	
490	{% for task in tasks %}
491	{{ loop.index }}.  [{{ task.status }}]{{ task.status }}[/{{ task.status }}]  {{ task.title }}
492	{% endfor %}
493	
494	{% if message %}[muted]{{ message }}[/muted]{% endif %}
495	"#;
496	
497	    let output = render(template, &report, &theme)?;
498	    print!("{}", output);
499	    Ok(())
500	}
501	```
502	
503	**Output (terminal):**
504	
505	```text
506	My Tasks
507	
508	1.  pending  Implement user authentication
509	2.  done     Review pull request #142
510	3.  pending  Update dependencies
511	
512	2 pending
513	```
514	
515	With colors, "pending" appears yellow, "done" appears green.
516	
517	---
518	
519	## Summary
520	
521	`standout-render` transforms CLI output from a chore into a pleasure:
522	
523	1. **Separation of concerns**: Data stays separate from templates. Templates define structure. Styles control appearance.
524	
525	2. **Fast iteration**: Hot reload means edit-and-see in seconds, not minutes. This changes what's practical.
526	
527	3. **Familiar tools**: MiniJinja for templates (Jinja2 syntax), CSS or YAML for styles. No new languages to learn.
528	
529	4. **Graceful degradation**: One template serves rich terminals, plain pipes, and everything in between.
530	
531	5. **Structured output for free**: JSON, YAML outputs work automatically from your serializable types.
532	
533	6. **Tabular layouts**: Declarative column definitions handle alignment, wrapping, truncation, and ANSI-awareness.
534	
535	The rendering system makes it practical to care about details. When iteration is fast and changes are safe, polish becomes achievable—not aspirational.
536	
537	For complete API details, see the [API documentation](https://docs.rs/standout-render).
538

1	# Minimal single-crate example
2	
3	This self-contained project is a compact way to see Standout's dispatch and
4	rendering pipeline. It keeps everything in one binary package for brevity; it
5	is not the recommended layout for an application with reusable logic.
6	
7	For production-shaped ownership, continue to the
8	[two-package worked application](production-shaped-example.md), where a
9	CLI-free library owns application behavior and a binary owns all CLI concerns.
10	
11	## File structure
12	
13	```text
14	my-todo/
15	├── Cargo.toml
16	└── src/
17	    ├── main.rs
18	    ├── templates/list.jinja
19	    └── styles/default.css
20	```
21	
22	## Cargo.toml
23	
24	```toml
25	[package]
26	name = "my-todo"
27	version = "0.1.0"
28	edition = "2021"
29	
30	[dependencies]
31	standout = "9"
32	clap = { version = "4", features = ["derive"] }
33	serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
34	anyhow = "1"
35	```
36	
37	## `src/main.rs`
38	
39	```rust
40	use clap::{CommandFactory, Parser, Subcommand};
41	use serde::Serialize;
42	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
43	use standout::{embed_styles, embed_templates, handler};
44	
45	#[derive(Parser)]
46	#[command(name = "my-todo")]
47	struct Cli {
48	    #[command(subcommand)]
49	    command: Option<Commands>,
50	}
51	
52	#[derive(Subcommand, Dispatch)]
53	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
54	enum Commands {
55	    /// List all todos. Running the binary with no command lists too.
56	    #[dispatch(pure, default)]
57	    List,
58	}
59	
60	#[derive(Serialize)]
61	struct TodoResult {
62	    todos: Vec<TodoView>,
63	}
64	
65	#[derive(Serialize)]
66	struct TodoView {
67	    title: String,
68	    status: String,
69	}
70	
71	mod handlers {
72	    use super::*;
73	
74	    // This is a CLI adapter returning view data. In a real application it
75	    // should call a CLI-free library rather than contain application behavior.
76	    #[handler]
77	    pub fn list(
78	        #[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext,
79	    ) -> Result<Output<TodoResult>, anyhow::Error> {
80	        Ok(Output::Render(TodoResult {
81	            todos: vec![
82	                TodoView { title: "Write documentation".into(), status: "done".into() },
83	                TodoView { title: "Ship v1.0".into(), status: "pending".into() },
84	            ],
85	        }))
86	    }
87	}
88	
89	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
90	    let app = App::builder()
91	        .version(env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))
92	        .templates(embed_templates!("src/templates"))
93	        .styles(embed_styles!("src/styles"))
94	        .default_theme("default")
95	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
96	        .build()?;
97	
98	    app.run(Cli::command(), std::env::args());
99	    Ok(())
100	}
101	```
102	
103	## `src/templates/list.jinja`
104	
105	```jinja
106	[title]My Todos[/title]
107	{% for todo in todos %}
108	[index]{{ loop.index }}.[/index] [{{ todo.status }}]{{ todo.title }}[/{{ todo.status }}]
109	{% endfor %}
110	```
111	
112	## `src/styles/default.css`
113	
114	```css
115	.title { color: cyan; font-weight: bold; }
116	.index { color: yellow; }
117	.done { color: gray; text-decoration: line-through; }
118	.pending { color: white; font-weight: bold; }
119	
120	@media (prefers-color-scheme: light) {
121	    .pending { color: black; }
122	}
123	```
124	
125	## Run it
126	
127	```bash
128	cargo run
129	cargo run -- list
130	cargo run -- list --output json
131	cargo run -- list --output text
132	```
133	
134	This demonstrates command dispatch, template rendering, structured output, hot
135	reload in debug builds, adaptive styles, and standout's themed `--help`, which
136	is on unless an application calls `.help_handling(false)`. It intentionally
137	does not teach package ownership or the testing pyramid; the
138	[production-shaped example](production-shaped-example.md) does.
139

1	# The `#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` Reference
2	
3	Two macros carry the blessed idiom. `#[derive(Dispatch)]` on an enum binds
4	command names to handler functions; `#[handler]` on a function turns it into
5	something the dispatcher can call. This page is the complete list of what each
6	one accepts.
7	
8	Both name mappings on this page — a variant name to a command name, and a
9	parameter name to a clap argument id — are contract, because they decide the
10	words a user types in a shell script. See
11	[What Is Contract](stability.md#4-the-two-name-mappings-a-user-types-on-the-command-line).
12	
13	## `#[derive(Dispatch)]`
14	
15	### The container attribute
16	
17	One attribute goes on the enum, and it is required:
18	
19	```rust,ignore
20	#[derive(Dispatch)]
21	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
22	enum Commands { /* … */ }
23	```
24	
25	`handlers = <module path>` names the module the derive looks each variant's
26	handler up in. Without it, expansion fails with `missing #[dispatch(handlers =
27	path)] attribute`.
28	
29	### From a variant name to a command name
30	
31	A variant registers under its **kebab-case** name — `ListUnits` becomes
32	`list-units` — which is the spelling clap's own derive gives the subcommand.
33	`#[dispatch(name = "…")]` renames one variant.
34	
35	A `name` may not be empty and may not contain `.`: dispatch splits registration
36	paths on `.`, so such a name would register a nested path no clap subcommand
37	declares. Nesting is `#[dispatch(nested)]`, below.
38	
39	A registered path that no clap subcommand can reach is a loud error naming the
40	path, raised by `App::run` and `App::verify_command` before dispatch.
41	
42	### From a variant name to a handler function
43	
44	The handler is looked up under the variant's **snake_case** name in the
45	`handlers` module — `ListUnits` calls `handlers::list_units`. Two attributes
46	change that:
47	
48	- `#[dispatch(pure)]` appends `__handler`, so the derive calls
49	  `handlers::list_units__handler` — the wrapper `#[handler]` generated. Use it
50	  whenever the handler function carries `#[handler]`, which is the blessed
51	  style. The derive registers through a closure taking `HandlerResult<T>`, so a
52	  `pure` handler must be annotated `-> Result<Output<T>, E>` or
53	  `-> Result<(), E>`; a plain `-> Result<T, E>` fails expansion. See
54	  [what `#[handler]` generates](#what-handler-generates).
55	- `#[dispatch(handler = <path>)]` names the function outright and ignores the
56	  inferred name.
57	
58	The two are mutually exclusive, and expansion rejects the pair with a message
59	naming both. Without `pure`, the derive calls the named function directly, so
60	that function must already have the dispatch signature.
61	
62	### Every variant attribute
63	
64	Several `#[dispatch(…)]` attributes may sit on one variant; they merge before
65	anything reads them.
66	
67	| Attribute | Form | What it does |
68	| --- | --- | --- |
69	| `name` | `name = "…"` | Registers the command under this name instead of the variant's kebab-case name. Not empty, no `.`. |
70	| `handler` | `handler = <path>` | Calls this function instead of the inferred one. Excludes `pure`. |
71	| `pure` | flag | The handler carries `#[handler]`: append `__handler` to the inferred name. Excludes `handler` and `simple`. |
72	| `simple` | flag | The handler takes only `&ArgMatches`, with no `&CommandContext`. Excludes `pure`. |
73	| `nested` | flag | The variant is a subcommand group. Requires a single-field tuple variant wrapping another `Dispatch` enum. |
74	| `skip` | flag | Registers nothing for this variant. |
75	| `default` | flag | Runs this command on a naked invocation. At most one variant per enum. |
76	| `template_name` | `template_name = "…"` | Names the template registry entry instead of using the convention. Excludes `silent`, `binary` and `structured_only`. |
77	| `silent` | flag | The command renders nothing. Excludes `binary`, `structured_only`, `template_name`. |
78	| `binary` | flag | The command writes bytes rather than a rendered page. Same exclusions. |
79	| `structured_only` | flag | The command has output only in the structured modes. Same exclusions. |
80	| `list_view` | flag | Renders through the framework's built-in `standout/list-view` template, unless `template_name` also appears, and attaches a tabular spec to the handler's `Output::Render`. |
81	| `item_type` | `item_type = "…"` | Names the `Tabular`-implementing item type `list_view` builds its spec from. |
82	| `questionnaire` | `questionnaire = <path>` | Resolves this questionnaire type before the handler runs. |
83	| `pre_dispatch` | `pre_dispatch = <path>` | Runs this hook before the handler. |
84	| `post_dispatch` | `post_dispatch = <path>` | Runs this hook after the handler, before rendering. |
85	| `post_output` | `post_output = <path>` | Runs this hook after the output is produced. |
86	| `pipe_to` | `pipe_to = "…"` | Sends the output to this command and keeps the original. |
87	| `pipe_through` | `pipe_through = "…"` | Replaces the output with this command's stdout. |
88	| `pipe_to_clipboard` | flag | Sends the output to the clipboard. |
89	
90	An unrecognized key fails expansion with a message listing every key above.
91	
92	### Nested commands
93	
94	`#[dispatch(nested)]` marks a variant that wraps another `Dispatch` enum:
95	
96	```rust,ignore
97	#[derive(Dispatch)]
98	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
99	enum Commands {
100	    #[dispatch(nested)]
101	    Pr(PrCommands),
102	}
103	```
104	
105	The derive registers the group rather than a command, and the inner enum's own
106	variants register beneath it. Registration paths are dot-joined as the
107	recursion descends, so `pr checks list` registers the path `pr.checks.list`.
108	
109	### How a command finds its template
110	
111	With no `template_name` and no absence marker (`silent`, `binary`,
112	`structured_only`), the template name **is** the registration path with each
113	`.` replaced by `/`, and **no extension appended**:
114	
115	| Registration path | Template name |
116	| --- | --- |
117	| `list` | `list` |
118	| `pr.checks.list` | `pr/checks/list` |
119	
120	The registry then resolves that name against `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`,
121	`.stpl` and `.txt`, in that priority order — so a nested `pr checks list`
122	command is rendered by `src/templates/pr/checks/list.jinja`. A name may be
123	looked up with or without an extension; the extension is stripped and the base
124	name retried.
125	
126	`#[dispatch(template_name = "…")]` replaces that name with a registry entry you
127	choose, which is how two commands share one template.
128	
129	## `#[handler]`
130	
131	### Parameter attributes
132	
133	Every typed parameter carries one of four attributes, references included: the
134	macro reads the value out of `ArgMatches` (or hands over the dispatcher's own
135	reference) by the attribute, never by the type, so a `&CommandContext` still
136	needs `#[ctx]` and an `&ArgMatches` still needs `#[matches]`.
137	
138	| Attribute | Type | Where the value comes from |
139	| --- | --- | --- |
140	| `#[flag]` | `bool` | `matches.get_flag(id)` |
141	| `#[arg]` | `T` | a required argument |
142	| `#[arg]` | `Option<T>` | an optional argument |
143	| `#[arg]` | `Vec<T>` | a repeated argument |
144	| `#[ctx]` | `&CommandContext` | the dispatcher |
145	| `#[matches]` | `&ArgMatches` | the dispatcher, unparsed |
146	
147	### From a parameter name to a clap argument id
148	
149	**Underscores become hyphens.** A parameter named `no_legend` reads the
150	argument whose id is `no-legend`.
151	
152	Clap's own derive ids an argument by the field name it comes from, so the two
153	disagree unless one of them says so. Either side can:
154	
155	```rust,ignore
156	#[arg(id = "no-legend")]        // on the clap-derive field
157	no_legend: bool,
158	
159	#[flag(name = "no_legend")]     // on the handler parameter
160	no_legend: bool,
161	```
162	
163	`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports the mismatch at build time rather than
164	leaving it to a runtime `get_flag` panic.
165	
166	A parameter named with a raw identifier drops the `r#` first, the way clap's
167	derive drops it from a field name: `r#type` reads the argument id `type`.
168	
169	### What `#[handler]` generates
170	
171	For `fn list`, four items:
172	
173	| Item | What it is |
174	| --- | --- |
175	| `list` | the original function, unchanged apart from the parameter attributes being removed — still directly callable from a test |
176	| `list__handler(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext)` | the wrapper that extracts the arguments and calls `list`. It returns **the function's own annotated return type**, verbatim |
177	| `list__expected_args() -> Vec<ExpectedArg>` | what `verify_command` reads |
178	| `list_Handler` | a unit struct implementing `Handler` — the registrable item |
179	
180	The `Result<T, E>` to `Output::Render` wrap happens inside `Handler::handle`,
181	not inside `list__handler`, and that is what makes the two registration methods
182	accept different things. `AppBuilder::command_with` takes an `impl Handler`, so
183	`handlers::list_Handler` works for any of the three return shapes.
184	`GroupBuilder::command_with` — which is what `#[derive(Dispatch)]` reaches —
185	takes a closure returning `HandlerResult<T>`, so it accepts
186	`handlers::list__handler` only when the function was annotated
187	`-> Result<Output<T>, E>` or `-> Result<(), E>`. The un-suffixed
188	`handlers::list` is registrable through neither.
189	
190	See the [handler contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for
191	the return types themselves.
192	
193	## A worked example
194	
195	Every attribute below is exercised by
196	`crates/standout-fixtures/src/derive_surface.rs`, which compiles under
197	`deny(warnings)` against a single `standout` dependency.
198	
199	```rust
200	use clap::{Arg, ArgAction, ArgMatches, Command};
201	use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
202	use standout::{handler, EmbeddedTemplates};
203	
204	#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
205	pub struct Units {
206	    pub names: Vec<String>,
207	}
208	
209	pub mod handlers {
210	    use super::*;
211	
212	    #[handler]
213	    pub fn list_units(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
214	        let mut names = vec!["ssh".to_string()];
215	        if all {
216	            names.push("cron".to_string());
217	        }
218	        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names }))
219	    }
220	
221	    #[handler]
222	    pub fn about(#[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
223	        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names: vec!["unitctl".to_string()] }))
224	    }
225	
226	    #[handler]
227	    pub fn reload(#[matches] _matches: &ArgMatches) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
228	        Ok(())
229	    }
230	}
231	
232	#[derive(Dispatch)]
233	#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
234	pub enum Commands {
235	    #[dispatch(pure, default)]
236	    ListUnits,
237	    #[dispatch(pure, name = "about-this")]
238	    About,
239	    #[dispatch(pure, silent)]
240	    Reload,
241	}
242	
243	const TEMPLATES: &[(&str, &str)] = &[
244	    ("list-units", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
245	    ("about-this", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
246	];
247	
248	/// The clap surface `Commands` is registered against. `Dispatch` connects a
249	/// variant to a handler; declaring the handler's arguments stays clap's job,
250	/// so `list-units` carries the `all` its handler reads.
251	fn command() -> Command {
252	    Command::new("unitctl")
253	        .subcommand(
254	            Command::new("list-units")
255	                .arg(Arg::new("all").long("all").action(ArgAction::SetTrue)),
256	        )
257	        .subcommand(Command::new("about-this"))
258	        .subcommand(Command::new("reload"))
259	}
260	
261	fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
262	    let app: App = App::builder()
263	        .templates(EmbeddedTemplates::new(TEMPLATES, ""))
264	        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
265	        .build()?;
266	    app.verify_command(&command())?;
267	    Ok(())
268	}
269	```
270	
271	`ListUnits` registers the command `list-units`, calls
272	`handlers::list_units__handler`, renders the registry entry `list-units`, and
273	runs on a naked invocation. Its `#[flag] all` parameter reads the clap argument
274	`all` that `command()` declares on that subcommand; `verify_command` is what
275	reports the two drifting apart, instead of leaving it to a `get_flag` panic on
276	the first invocation. `About` registers `about-this` and renders the
277	entry of the same name, because `name` changes the registration path and the
278	convention follows it. `Reload` registers `reload`, calls
279	`handlers::reload__handler` and renders nothing, so it needs no template.
280

`.stpl` and `.txt`, in that priority order — so a nested `pr checks list`
command is rendered by `src/templates/pr/checks/list.jinja`. A name may be
looked up with or without an extension; the extension is stripped and the base
name retried.

`#[dispatch(template_name = "…")]` replaces that name with a registry entry you
choose, which is how two commands share one template.

## `#[handler]`

### Parameter attributes

Every typed parameter carries one of four attributes, references included: the
macro reads the value out of `ArgMatches` (or hands over the dispatcher's own
reference) by the attribute, never by the type, so a `&CommandContext` still
needs `#[ctx]` and an `&ArgMatches` still needs `#[matches]`.

| Attribute | Type | Where the value comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `#[flag]` | `bool` | `matches.get_flag(id)` |
| `#[arg]` | `T` | a required argument |
| `#[arg]` | `Option<T>` | an optional argument |
| `#[arg]` | `Vec<T>` | a repeated argument |
| `#[ctx]` | `&CommandContext` | the dispatcher |
| `#[matches]` | `&ArgMatches` | the dispatcher, unparsed |

### From a parameter name to a clap argument id

**Underscores become hyphens.** A parameter named `no_legend` reads the
argument whose id is `no-legend`.

Clap's own derive ids an argument by the field name it comes from, so the two
disagree unless one of them says so. Either side can:

```rust,ignore
#[arg(id = "no-legend")]        // on the clap-derive field
no_legend: bool,

#[flag(name = "no_legend")]     // on the handler parameter
no_legend: bool,
```

`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports the mismatch at build time rather than
leaving it to a runtime `get_flag` panic.

A parameter named with a raw identifier drops the `r#` first, the way clap's
derive drops it from a field name: `r#type` reads the argument id `type`.

### What `#[handler]` generates

For `fn list`, four items:

| Item | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `list` | the original function, unchanged apart from the parameter attributes being removed — still directly callable from a test |
| `list__handler(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext)` | the wrapper that extracts the arguments and calls `list`. It returns **the function's own annotated return type**, verbatim |
| `list__expected_args() -> Vec<ExpectedArg>` | what `verify_command` reads |
| `list_Handler` | a unit struct implementing `Handler` — the registrable item |

The `Result<T, E>` to `Output::Render` wrap happens inside `Handler::handle`,
not inside `list__handler`, and that is what makes the two registration methods
accept different things. `AppBuilder::command_with` takes an `impl Handler`, so
`handlers::list_Handler` works for any of the three return shapes.
`GroupBuilder::command_with` — which is what `#[derive(Dispatch)]` reaches —
takes a closure returning `HandlerResult<T>`, so it accepts
`handlers::list__handler` only when the function was annotated
`-> Result<Output<T>, E>` or `-> Result<(), E>`. The un-suffixed
`handlers::list` is registrable through neither.

See the [handler contract](../crates/dispatch/topics/handler-contract.md) for
the return types themselves.

## A worked example

Every attribute below is exercised by
`crates/standout-fixtures/src/derive_surface.rs`, which compiles under
`deny(warnings)` against a single `standout` dependency.

```rust
use clap::{Arg, ArgAction, ArgMatches, Command};
use standout::cli::{App, CommandContext, Dispatch, Output};
use standout::{handler, EmbeddedTemplates};

#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
pub struct Units {
    pub names: Vec<String>,
}

pub mod handlers {
    use super::*;

    #[handler]
    pub fn list_units(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
        let mut names = vec!["ssh".to_string()];
        if all {
            names.push("cron".to_string());
        }
        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names }))
    }

    #[handler]
    pub fn about(#[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<Units>, anyhow::Error> {
        Ok(Output::Render(Units { names: vec!["unitctl".to_string()] }))
    }

    #[handler]
    pub fn reload(#[matches] _matches: &ArgMatches) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
        Ok(())
    }
}

#[derive(Dispatch)]
#[dispatch(handlers = handlers)]
pub enum Commands {
    #[dispatch(pure, default)]
    ListUnits,
    #[dispatch(pure, name = "about-this")]
    About,
    #[dispatch(pure, silent)]
    Reload,
}

const TEMPLATES: &[(&str, &str)] = &[
    ("list-units", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
    ("about-this", "{{ names | join(', ') }}"),
];

/// The clap surface `Commands` is registered against. `Dispatch` connects a
/// variant to a handler; declaring the handler's arguments stays clap's job,
/// so `list-units` carries the `all` its handler reads.
fn command() -> Command {
    Command::new("unitctl")
        .subcommand(
            Command::new("list-units")
                .arg(Arg::new("all").long("all").action(ArgAction::SetTrue)),
        )
        .subcommand(Command::new("about-this"))
        .subcommand(Command::new("reload"))
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let app: App = App::builder()
        .templates(EmbeddedTemplates::new(TEMPLATES, ""))
        .commands(Commands::dispatch_config())?
        .build()?;
    app.verify_command(&command())?;
    Ok(())
}
```

`ListUnits` registers the command `list-units`, calls
`handlers::list_units__handler`, renders the registry entry `list-units`, and
runs on a naked invocation. Its `#[flag] all` parameter reads the clap argument
`all` that `command()` declares on that subcommand; `verify_command` is what
reports the two drifting apart, instead of leaving it to a `get_flag` panic on
the first invocation. `About` registers `about-this` and renders the
entry of the same name, because `name` changes the registration path and the
convention follows it. `Reload` registers `reload`, calls
`handlers::reload__handler` and renders nothing, so it needs no template.

1	# Templating
2	
3	`standout-render` uses a two-pass templating system that combines a template engine for logic and data binding with a custom BBCode-like syntax for styling. This separation keeps templates readable while providing full control over both content and presentation.
4	
5	The default engine is MiniJinja (Jinja2-compatible), but alternative engines are available. See [Template Engines](template-engines.md) for options including a lightweight `SimpleEngine` for reduced binary size.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Two-Pass Rendering Pipeline
10	
11	Templates are processed in two distinct passes:
12	
13	```text
14	Template + Data → [Pass 1: MiniJinja] → Text with style tags → [Pass 2: BBParser] → Final output
15	```
16	
17	**Pass 1 - MiniJinja**: Standard template processing. Variables are substituted, control flow executes, filters apply.
18	
19	**Pass 2 - BBParser**: Style tag processing. Bracket-notation tags are converted to ANSI escape codes (or stripped, depending on output mode).
20	
21	### Pipeline Example
22	
23	```text
24	Template:     [title]{{ name }}[/title] has {{ count }} items
25	Data:         { name: "Report", count: 42 }
26	
27	After Pass 1: [title]Report[/title] has 42 items
28	After Pass 2: \x1b[1;36mReport\x1b[0m has 42 items  (or plain: "Report has 42 items")
29	```
30	
31	This separation means:
32	
33	- Template logic (loops, conditionals) is handled by MiniJinja—a mature, well-documented engine
34	- Style application is a simple, predictable transformation
35	- You can debug each pass independently
36	
37	---
38	
39	## MiniJinja Basics
40	
41	MiniJinja implements Jinja2 syntax, a widely-used templating language. Here's a quick overview:
42	
43	### Variables
44	
45	```jinja
46	{{ variable }}
47	{{ object.field }}
48	{{ list[0] }}
49	```
50	
51	### Control Flow
52	
53	```jinja
54	{% if condition %}
55	  Show this
56	{% elif other_condition %}
57	  Show that
58	{% else %}
59	  Default
60	{% endif %}
61	
62	{% for item in items %}
63	  {{ loop.index }}. {{ item.name }}
64	{% endfor %}
65	```
66	
67	### Filters
68	
69	```jinja
70	{{ name | upper }}
71	{{ list | length }}
72	{{ value | default("N/A") }}
73	{{ text | truncate(20) }}
74	```
75	
76	### Comments
77	
78	```jinja
79	{# This is a comment and won't appear in output #}
80	```
81	
82	For comprehensive MiniJinja documentation, see the [MiniJinja documentation](https://docs.rs/minijinja).
83	
84	### Booleans and None
85	
86	Standout renders these the Rust way — `true`, `false`, `none` — not the Jinja2
87	way MiniJinja itself uses (`True`, `False`, `None`). This holds for
88	interpolation, loop and `set` bindings, `| string`, `| join`, sequence and map
89	literals, standout's own filters, and table cells:
90	
91	```jinja
92	{{ flag }}                {# true #}
93	{{ missing }}             {# none #}
94	{{ flags }}               {# [true, false, none] #}
95	{{ flags | join(", ") }}  {# true, false, none #}
96	```
97	
98	Two exceptions:
99	
100	- The `~` concatenation operator formats inside MiniJinja's evaluator, which
101	  exposes no hook: `{{ "x" ~ flag }}` yields `xTrue`. Write `{{ "x" }}{{ flag }}`
102	  or `{{ "x" ~ flag | string }}`.
103	- Structured output (JSON, YAML, XML, CSV) skips templates entirely and
104	  serializes your data directly, so those modes follow their format's own rules.
105	
106	If you build a `minijinja::Environment` yourself, use
107	`standout_render::template::new_environment()` — or call `register_filters` on
108	your own environment, which installs the same spelling.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## The Trailing-Newline Contract
113	
114	Two things happen to the newline at the end of a template, and together they
115	are observable in the bytes a script reads, so they are stated here rather than
116	discovered by probing.
117	
118	**The engine consumes exactly one final newline.** This is Jinja's rule and
119	MiniJinja keeps it. A template file ending in a single `\n` renders with no
120	trailing newline at all; a file ending in two renders with one.
121	
122	| Template source | Rendered string |
123	| --- | --- |
124	| `{{ name }}` | `x` |
125	| `{{ name }}\n` | `x` |
126	| `{{ name }}\n\n` | `x\n` |
127	| `{{ name }}\n\n\n` | `x\n\n` |
128	
129	**The process edge appends exactly one newline.** `App::run` writes a handled
130	command's text with `writeln!`, so what reaches stdout is the rendered string
131	plus one `\n` — whatever the template ended with.
132	
133	The practical consequence: a template that ends with one newline and a template
134	that ends with none produce identical bytes. To end a page with a blank line,
135	the template needs *two* trailing newlines. Every editor that adds a final
136	newline on save is therefore invisible here, which is the reason the rule is
137	worth stating.
138	
139	`standout-render/tests/trailing_newline.rs` pins the engine half;
140	`final_emission_routes_success_and_diagnostics_to_distinct_streams` in
141	`standout/src/cli/builder/execution.rs` pins the process half.
142	
143	---
144	
145	## Style Tags
146	
147	Style tags use BBCode-like bracket notation to apply named styles from your theme:
148	
149	```jinja
150	[style-name]content to style[/style-name]
151	```
152	
153	### Basic Usage
154	
155	```jinja
156	[title]Report Summary[/title]
157	[error]Something went wrong![/error]
158	[muted]Last updated: {{ timestamp }}[/muted]
159	```
160	
161	### Nesting
162	
163	Tags can nest properly:
164	
165	```jinja
166	[outer][inner]nested content[/inner][/outer]
167	```
168	
169	### Spanning Lines
170	
171	Tags can span multiple lines:
172	
173	```jinja
174	[panel]
175	This is a multi-line
176	block of styled content
177	[/panel]
178	```
179	
180	### With Template Logic
181	
182	Style tags and MiniJinja work together seamlessly:
183	
184	```jinja
185	[title]{% if custom_title %}{{ custom_title }}{% else %}Default Title{% endif %}[/title]
186	
187	{% for task in tasks %}
188	[{{ task.status }}]{{ task.title }}[/{{ task.status }}]
189	{% endfor %}
190	```
191	
192	The second example shows dynamic style names—the style applied depends on the value of `task.status`.
193	
194	---
195	
196	## Processing Modes
197	
198	Pass 2 (BBParser) processes style tags differently based on the output mode:
199	
200	| Mode | Behavior | Use Case |
201	| ------ | ---------- | ---------- |
202	| `Term` | Replace tags with ANSI escape codes | Rich terminal output |
203	| `Text` | Strip tags completely | Plain text, pipes, files |
204	| `TermDebug` | Keep tags as literal text | Debugging, testing |
205	
206	### Processing Modes Example
207	
208	Template: `[title]Hello[/title]`
209	
210	- **Term**: `\x1b[1;36mHello\x1b[0m` (rendered as cyan bold)
211	- **Text**: `Hello`
212	- **TermDebug**: `[title]Hello[/title]`
213	
214	### Setting the Mode
215	
216	```rust
217	use standout_render::{render_with_output, OutputMode};
218	
219	// Rich terminal
220	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term)?;
221	
222	// Plain text
223	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Text)?;
224	
225	// Debug (tags visible)
226	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::TermDebug)?;
227	
228	// Auto-detect based on TTY
229	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Auto)?;
230	```
231	
232	### Auto Mode
233	
234	`OutputMode::Auto` detects the appropriate mode:
235	
236	- If stdout is a TTY with color support → `Term`
237	- If stdout is a pipe or redirect → `Text`
238	
239	> **For standout framework users:** The framework's `--output` CLI flag automatically sets the output mode. See standout documentation for details.
240	
241	---
242	
243	## Built-in Filters
244	
245	Beyond MiniJinja's standard filters, `standout-render` provides formatting filters:
246	
247	### Column Formatting
248	
249	```jinja
250	{{ value | col(10) }}                              {# pad/truncate to 10 chars #}
251	{{ value | col(20, align="right") }}               {# right-align in 20 chars #}
252	{{ value | col(15, truncate="middle") }}           {# truncate in middle #}
253	{{ value | col(15, truncate="start", ellipsis="...") }}
254	```
255	
256	### Padding
257	
258	```jinja
259	{{ "42" | pad_left(8) }}      {# "      42" #}
260	{{ "hi" | pad_right(8) }}     {# "hi      " #}
261	{{ "hi" | pad_center(8) }}    {# "   hi   " #}
262	```
263	
264	### Truncation
265	
266	```jinja
267	{{ long_text | truncate_at(20) }}                   {# "Very long text th..." #}
268	{{ path | truncate_at(30, "middle", "...") }}      {# "/home/.../file.txt" #}
269	{{ text | truncate_at(20, "start") }}              {# "...end of the text" #}
270	```
271	
272	### Display Width
273	
274	```jinja
275	{% if value | display_width > 20 %}
276	  {{ value | truncate_at(20) }}
277	{% else %}
278	  {{ value }}
279	{% endif %}
280	```
281	
282	Returns visual width (handles Unicode—CJK characters count as 2).
283	
284	### Style Application
285	
286	```jinja
287	{{ value | style_as("error") }}                    {# wraps in [error]...[/error] #}
288	{{ task.status | style_as(task.status) }}         {# dynamic: [pending]pending[/pending] #}
289	```
290	
291	---
292	
293	## Template Registry
294	
295	When using the `Renderer` struct, templates are resolved by name through a registry:
296	
297	```rust
298	use standout_render::Renderer;
299	
300	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(theme)?;
301	
302	// Add inline template
303	renderer.add_template("greeting", "Hello, [name]{{ name }}[/name]!")?;
304	
305	// Add directory of templates
306	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
307	
308	// Render by name
309	let output = renderer.render("greeting", &data)?;
310	```
311	
312	### Resolution Priority
313	
314	1. **Inline templates** (added via `add_template()`)
315	2. **Directory templates** (from `add_template_dir()`)
316	
317	### File Extensions
318	
319	Supported extensions (in priority order): `.jinja`, `.jinja2`, `.j2`, `.stpl`, `.txt`
320	
321	When you request `"report"`, the registry checks:
322	
323	- Inline template named `"report"`
324	- `report.jinja` in registered directories
325	- `report.jinja2`, `report.j2`, `report.stpl`, `report.txt` (lower priority)
326	
327	The `.stpl` extension is for SimpleEngine templates. See [Template Engines](template-engines.md) for details.
328	
329	### Template Names
330	
331	Template names are derived from relative paths:
332	
333	```text
334	templates/
335	├── greeting.jinja       → "greeting"
336	├── reports/
337	│   └── summary.jinja    → "reports/summary"
338	└── errors/
339	    └── 404.jinja        → "errors/404"
340	```
341	
342	---
343	
344	## Including Templates
345	
346	Templates can include other templates using MiniJinja's include syntax:
347	
348	```jinja
349	{# main.jinja #}
350	[title]{{ title }}[/title]
351	
352	{% include "partials/header.jinja" %}
353	
354	{% for item in items %}
355	  {% include "partials/item.jinja" %}
356	{% endfor %}
357	
358	{% include "partials/footer.jinja" %}
359	```
360	
361	This enables reusable components across your application.
362	
363	---
364	
365	## Context Variables
366	
367	Beyond your data, you can inject additional context into templates:
368	
369	```rust
370	use standout_render::{render_with_vars, OutputMode};
371	use std::collections::HashMap;
372	
373	let mut vars = HashMap::new();
374	vars.insert("version", "1.0.0");
375	vars.insert("app_name", "MyApp");
376	
377	let output = render_with_vars(
378	    "{{ app_name }} v{{ version }}: {{ message }}",
379	    &data,
380	    &theme,
381	    OutputMode::Term,
382	    vars,
383	)?;
384	```
385	
386	When handler data and context variables have the same key, **handler data wins**. Context is supplementary.
387	
388	---
389	
390	## Structured Output
391	
392	For machine-readable output (JSON, YAML, CSV), templates are bypassed entirely:
393	
394	```rust
395	use standout_render::{render_auto, OutputMode};
396	
397	// Template is used for Term/Text modes
398	// Data is serialized directly for Json/Yaml/Csv
399	let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
400	```
401	
402	| Mode | Behavior |
403	| ------ | ---------- |
404	| `Term` | Render template, apply styles |
405	| `Text` | Render template, strip styles |
406	| `TermDebug` | Render template, keep style tags |
407	| `Json` | `serde_json::to_string_pretty(data)` |
408	| `Yaml` | `serde_yaml::to_string(data)` |
409	| `Csv` | Flatten and format as CSV |
410	
411	This means your serializable data types automatically support structured output without additional code.
412	
413	---
414	
415	## Validation
416	
417	Check templates for unknown style tags before deploying:
418	
419	```rust
420	use standout_render::validate_template;
421	
422	let errors = validate_template(template, &sample_data, &theme);
423	if !errors.is_empty() {
424	    for error in &errors {
425	        eprintln!("Unknown style tag: [{}]", error.tag_name);
426	    }
427	}
428	```
429	
430	Validation catches:
431	
432	- Misspelled style names
433	- References to undefined styles
434	- Mismatched opening/closing tags
435	
436	---
437	
438	## API Reference
439	
440	### Render Functions
441	
442	```rust
443	use standout_render::{
444	    render,                  // Basic: template + data + theme
445	    render_with_output,      // With explicit output mode
446	    render_with_mode,        // With output mode + color mode
447	    render_with_vars,        // With extra context variables
448	    render_auto,             // Auto-dispatch template vs serialize
449	    render_auto_with_context,
450	};
451	
452	// Basic
453	let output = render(template, &data, &theme)?;
454	
455	// With output mode
456	let output = render_with_output(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term)?;
457	
458	// With color mode override (for testing)
459	let output = render_with_mode(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Term, ColorMode::Dark)?;
460	
461	// Auto (template for text modes, serialize for structured)
462	let output = render_auto(template, &data, &theme, OutputMode::Json)?;
463	```
464	
465	### Renderer Struct
466	
467	```rust
468	use standout_render::Renderer;
469	
470	let mut renderer = Renderer::new(theme)?;
471	renderer.add_template("name", "content")?;
472	renderer.add_template_dir("./templates")?;
473	
474	let output = renderer.render("name", &data)?;
475	let output = renderer.render_with_mode("name", &data, OutputMode::Text)?;
476	```
477

1	# The Handler Contract
2	
3	Handlers are shell adapters: they map parsed CLI input to application calls and
4	return serializable CLI-owned view data. Keep reusable behavior in a CLI-free
5	library. The handler contract is designed to be **explicit** rather than
6	permissive, so adapters remain testable and decoupled from output formatting.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## Quick Start: The `#[handler]` Macro
11	
12	For most handlers, use the `#[handler]` macro to write typed adapter functions:
13	
14	```rust,ignore
15	use standout_macros::handler;
16	
17	#[handler]
18	pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool, #[arg] limit: Option<usize>) -> Result<Vec<Item>, anyhow::Error> {
19	    storage::list(all, limit)
20	}
21	```
22	
23	The macro leaves `list` alone and adds three items beside it:
24	
25	| Item | What it is |
26	| --- | --- |
27	| `list__handler(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext)` | reads the arguments out of `ArgMatches` and calls `list`. It returns **the annotated return type verbatim** — here `Result<Vec<Item>, anyhow::Error>`, not `HandlerResult<Vec<Item>>` |
28	| `list__expected_args() -> Vec<ExpectedArg>` | what `App::verify_command` reads |
29	| `list_Handler` | a unit struct implementing [`Handler`](#the-handler-trait) — **the registrable item** |
30	
31	The `Result<T, E>` to `Output::Render` wrap happens inside `list_Handler`'s
32	`Handler::handle`, which calls `IntoHandlerResult::into_handler_result` on
33	whatever `list__handler` returned. It is not applied by `list__handler` itself.
34	Only registration of `list_Handler` runs that wrap. `#[derive(Dispatch)]` does
35	not reach the trait object at all: it registers the closure
36	`handlers::list__handler` through `GroupBuilder::command_with`, so nothing
37	calls `Handler::handle` and the annotated return type has to be a
38	`HandlerResult` shape already. That is the difference the next two tables
39	spell out.
40	
41	The un-suffixed `handlers::list` is not registrable — it has the wrong
42	signature by design, so that a test can call it directly. Which of the other
43	two items you register depends on the method:
44	
45	| Method | What it takes | What to pass |
46	| --- | --- | --- |
47	| `AppBuilder::command_with` | `impl Handler` | `handlers::list_Handler` |
48	| `GroupBuilder::command` / `command_with`, and therefore `#[derive(Dispatch)]` | a closure returning `HandlerResult<T>` | `handlers::list__handler` |
49	
50	That second row constrains the return type, and it is the one place the two
51	registration paths genuinely differ. `list__handler` returns the annotated type
52	verbatim, so it satisfies `HandlerResult<T>` only when the function was written
53	`-> Result<Output<T>, E>` (or `-> Result<(), E>`, whose wrapper returns
54	`HandlerResult<()>`). **A handler annotated `-> Result<T, E>` cannot be
55	registered through `#[derive(Dispatch)]`**: expansion fails with `expected
56	list__handler to return Result<Output<_>, Error>, but it returns Result<Items,
57	Error>`. Write it `-> Result<Output<T>, E>`, or register `list_Handler` through
58	`AppBuilder::command_with`, where `Handler::handle` applies the wrap for you.
59	
60	The three return shapes, and the original functions still being callable:
61	
62	```rust
63	use standout::cli::{CommandContext, Output};
64	use standout::handler;
65	
66	#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
67	pub struct Items {
68	    pub names: Vec<String>,
69	}
70	
71	/// `Handler::Output` is `Items`; `handle` wraps the value in `Output::Render`.
72	#[handler]
73	pub fn list(#[flag] all: bool) -> Result<Items, anyhow::Error> {
74	    let mut names = vec!["ssh".to_string()];
75	    if all {
76	        names.push("cron".to_string());
77	    }
78	    Ok(Items { names })
79	}
80	
81	/// `Handler::Output` is `Items`; the `Output` passes through untouched.
82	#[handler]
83	pub fn about(#[ctx] _ctx: &CommandContext) -> Result<Output<Items>, anyhow::Error> {
84	    Ok(Output::Render(Items { names: vec!["unitctl".to_string()] }))
85	}
86	
87	/// `Handler::Output` is `()`; `handle` produces `Output::Silent`.
88	#[handler]
89	pub fn reload(#[flag] _force: bool) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
90	    Ok(())
91	}
92	
93	fn main() {
94	    // No ArgMatches, no dispatcher: the annotated function is what a unit test calls.
95	    assert_eq!(list(true).unwrap().names, ["ssh", "cron"]);
96	    reload(false).unwrap();
97	}
98	```
99	
100	Every `#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` attribute is listed in the
101	[`#[dispatch(…)]` and `#[handler]` reference](../../../topics/dispatch-attributes.md).
102	
103	**Parameter Annotations:**
104	
105	| Annotation            | Type              | Extraction                    |
106	| --------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------- |
107	| `#[flag]`             | `bool`            | `matches.get_flag("name")`    |
108	| `#[flag(name = "x")]` | `bool`            | `matches.get_flag("x")`       |
109	| `#[arg]`              | `T`               | Required argument             |
110	| `#[arg]`              | `Option<T>`       | Optional argument             |
111	| `#[arg]`              | `Vec<T>`          | Multiple values               |
112	| `#[arg(name = "x")]`  | `T`               | Argument with custom CLI name |
113	| `#[ctx]`              | `&CommandContext` | Access to context             |
114	| `#[matches]`          | `&ArgMatches`     | Raw matches (escape hatch)    |
115	
116	Without `name = "x"`, the argument id is the parameter name with underscores
117	turned into hyphens: `no_legend` reads the argument id `no-legend`. Clap's own
118	derive ids an argument by the field name it comes from, so a clap-derive
119	`no_legend` field declares `#[arg(id = "no-legend")]` to meet the handler, or
120	the handler parameter takes the field's id with `#[flag(name = "no_legend")]`.
121	`app.verify_command(&cmd)` reports the mismatch instead of leaving it to a
122	runtime `get_flag` panic. A parameter named with a raw identifier drops the
123	`r#` first, the way clap's derive drops it from a field name: `r#type` reads
124	the argument id `type`.
125	
126	**Return Type Handling:** the function must return `Result<T, E>`; the macro
127	rejects anything else with `handler must return Result<T, E>`. What `T` is
128	decides what `Handler::Output` becomes and whether anything is wrapped.
129	
130	| Annotated return type | `Handler::Output` | What `handle` produces |
131	| --- | --- | --- |
132	| `Result<T, E>` | `T` | `Ok(value)` wrapped in `Output::Render(value)` |
133	| `Result<Output<T>, E>` (that is, `HandlerResult<T>`) | `T` | the `Output` you returned, unchanged |
134	| `Result<(), E>` | `()` | `Output::Silent` |
135	
136	> **Testing:** The original function is preserved, so you can test directly: `list(true, Some(10))`.
137

140	## The Handler Trait
141	
142	```rust,ignore
143	pub trait Handler {
144	    type Output: Serialize;
145	    fn handle(&mut self, matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Self::Output>;
146	}
147	```
148	
149	Key characteristics:
150	
151	- **Mutable self**: `&mut self` allows direct state modification
152	- **Output must be Serialize**: Needed for JSON/YAML modes and template context
153	
154	Implementing the trait directly is useful when your handler needs internal state—database connections, configuration, caches, etc.
155	
156	### Example: Struct Handler with State
157	
158	```rust,ignore
159	use standout_dispatch::{Handler, Output, CommandContext, HandlerResult};
160	use clap::ArgMatches;
161	use serde::Serialize;
162	
163	struct CachingDatabase {
164	    connection: Connection,
165	    cache: HashMap<String, Vec<Row>>,
166	}
167	
168	impl CachingDatabase {
169	    fn query_with_cache(&mut self, sql: &str) -> Result<Vec<Row>, Error> {
170	        if let Some(cached) = self.cache.get(sql) {
171	            return Ok(cached.clone());
172	        }
173	        let result = self.connection.execute(sql)?;
174	        self.cache.insert(sql.to_string(), result.clone());
175	        Ok(result)
176	    }
177	}
178	
179	impl Handler for CachingDatabase {
180	    type Output = Vec<Row>;
181	
182	    fn handle(&mut self, matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Row>> {
183	        let query: &String = matches.get_one("query").unwrap();
184	        let rows = self.query_with_cache(query)?;  // &mut self works!
185	        Ok(Output::Render(rows))
186	    }
187	}
188	```

192	## Closure Handlers
193	
194	Most handlers are simple closures using `FnHandler`:
195	
196	```rust,ignore
197	use standout_dispatch::{FnHandler, Output, HandlerResult};
198	
199	let mut counter = 0;
200	
201	let handler = FnHandler::new(move |_matches, _ctx| {
202	    counter += 1;  // Mutation works!
203	    Ok(Output::Render(counter))
204	});
205	```
206	
207	The closure signature:
208	
209	```rust,ignore
210	fn(&ArgMatches, &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<T>
211	where T: Serialize
212	```
213	
214	Closures are `FnMut`, allowing captured variables to be mutated.

218	## SimpleFnHandler (No Context Needed)
219	
220	When your handler doesn't need `CommandContext`, use `SimpleFnHandler` for a cleaner signature:
221	
222	```rust,ignore
223	use standout_dispatch::SimpleFnHandler;
224	
225	let handler = SimpleFnHandler::new(|matches| {
226	    let verbose = matches.get_flag("verbose");
227	    let items = storage::list()?;
228	    Ok(ListResult { items, verbose })
229	});
230	```
231	
232	The closure signature:
233	
234	```rust,ignore
235	fn(&ArgMatches) -> Result<T, E>
236	where T: Serialize, E: Into<anyhow::Error>
237	```
238	
239	`SimpleFnHandler` automatically wraps the result in `Output::Render` via `IntoHandlerResult`.

243	## IntoHandlerResult Trait
244	
245	The `IntoHandlerResult` trait enables handlers to return `Result<T, E>` directly instead of `HandlerResult<T>`:
246	
247	```rust,ignore
248	use standout_dispatch::IntoHandlerResult;
249	
250	// Before: explicit Output wrapping
251	fn list(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
252	    let items = storage::list()?;
253	    Ok(Output::Render(items))
254	}
255	
256	// After: automatic conversion
257	fn list(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> impl IntoHandlerResult<Vec<Item>> {
258	    storage::list()  // Result<Vec<Item>, Error> auto-converts
259	}
260	```
261	
262	The trait is implemented for:
263	
264	- `Result<T, E>` where `E: Into<anyhow::Error>` → wraps `Ok(t)` in `Output::Render(t)`
265	- `HandlerResult<T>` → passes through unchanged
266	
267	This is used internally by `SimpleFnHandler` and the `#[handler]` macro.
268

270	
271	## HandlerResult
272	
273	`HandlerResult<T>` is a standard `Result` type:
274	
275	```rust,ignore
276	pub type HandlerResult<T> = Result<Output<T>, anyhow::Error>;
277	```
278	
279	The `?` operator works naturally for error propagation:
280	
281	```rust,ignore
282	fn list_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<Items> {
283	    let items = storage::load()?;           // Propagates errors
284	    let filtered = filter_items(&items)?;   // Propagates errors
285	    Ok(Output::Render(Items { filtered }))
286	}
287	```
288	
289	### Authoritative external failures
290	
291	When a handler delegates to another executable and the application's contract
292	requires that executable's exact nonzero status and stderr, return the public
293	`ExternalFailure` type through the same `HandlerResult` seam:
294	
295	```rust,ignore
296	let failure = ExternalFailure::new(128, git_stderr)?;
297	Err(failure.into())
298	```
299	
300	Construction rejects status `0`. Standout recognizes only this concrete type,
301	preserves its diagnostic verbatim, and exposes it as `RunErrorKind::External`.
302	Ordinary handler errors still use status `1`; this is not a general exit-code
303	mapping mechanism. Handlers must not print or call `process::exit` themselves.
304

306	
307	## The Output Enum
308	
309	`Output<T>` represents what a handler produces:
310	
311	```rust,ignore
312	#[non_exhaustive]
313	pub enum Output<T: Serialize> {
314	    Render(T),
315	    Silent,
316	    Binary { data: Vec<u8>, filename: String },
317	    Artifact(Artifact<T>),
318	}
319	```
320	
321	`Output` is `#[non_exhaustive]`: matches on it need a `_` arm so later shapes
322	can be added without breaking downstream code.
323	
324	### Output::Render(T)
325	
326	The common case. Data is passed to the render function:
327	
328	```rust,ignore
329	#[derive(Serialize)]
330	struct ListResult {
331	    items: Vec<Item>,
332	    total: usize,
333	}
334	
335	fn list_handler(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ListResult> {
336	    let items = storage::list()?;
337	    Ok(Output::Render(ListResult {
338	        total: items.len(),
339	        items,
340	    }))
341	}
342	```
343	
344	### Output::Silent
345	
346	No output produced. Useful for commands with side effects only:
347	
348	```rust,ignore
349	fn delete_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<()> {
350	    let id: &String = matches.get_one("id").unwrap();
351	    storage::delete(id)?;
352	    Ok(Output::Silent)
353	}
354	```
355	
356	Silent behavior:
357	
358	- Post-output hooks still receive `RenderedOutput::Silent`
359	- Render function is not called
360	- Nothing prints to stdout
361	
362	### Output::Binary
363	
364	Raw bytes for file output:
365	
366	```rust,ignore
367	fn export_handler(matches: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<()> {
368	    let data = generate_report()?;
369	    let pdf_bytes = render_to_pdf(&data)?;
370	
371	    Ok(Output::Binary {
372	        data: pdf_bytes,
373	        filename: "report.pdf".into(),
374	    })
375	}
376	```
377	
378	Binary output bypasses the render function entirely.
379	
380	The filename is a **hint for the caller**, not permission to write. Without
381	`--output-file-path`, `run()` sends the bytes to stdout and touches no file. If
382	you want the framework to write the suggested destination, use `Output::Artifact`
383	— that opt-in is the whole difference between the two shapes.
384	
385	### Output::Artifact
386	
387	Owned bytes plus an application-owned report, for commands that produce a file
388	*and* have something to say about it. `Output::Binary` cannot carry a report,
389	and nothing renders after its write, so a command that wants to say "exported 12
390	rows to /tmp/report.csv (2 warnings)" would otherwise have to write the file
391	itself — pulling destination policy back into the application core.
392	
393	```rust,ignore
394	use standout::cli::{Artifact, HandlerResult, Output};
395	
396	#[derive(Serialize)]
397	struct ExportReport {
398	    exported: usize,
399	    warnings: Vec<Warning>,
400	}
401	
402	fn export_handler(_m: &ArgMatches, _ctx: &CommandContext) -> HandlerResult<ExportReport> {
403	    let export = core::export_csv()?;   // bytes + facts, no filesystem
404	
405	    Ok(Output::Artifact(
406	        Artifact::new(export.csv)
407	            .suggest_destination(export.suggested_filename)
408	            .with_report(ExportReport {
409	                exported: export.rows,
410	                warnings: export.warnings,
411	            }),
412	    ))
413	}
414	```
415	
416	Who owns what:
417	
418	| Concern | Owner |
419	| --- | --- |
420	| Artifact bytes | Application |
421	| Suggested destination | Application (a suggestion) |
422	| Semantic report and warning taxonomy | Application |
423	| Destination selection | Framework |
424	| The write and its failure | Framework |
425	| Receipt (completed destination) | Framework |
426	
427	#### Destination policy
428	
429	Standout selects the destination deterministically:
430	
431	1. the explicit `--output-file-path` override;
432	2. the artifact's `suggest_destination(...)`, if the application opted in;
433	3. stdout, if the application opted in with `allow_stdout()`.
434	
435	If none applies, the run fails with `FinalWrite(Artifact)` rather than inventing
436	a file or dropping the bytes. All three steps share that one failure path.
437	
438	#### Write first, report second
439	
440	Standout writes, then renders the report from a fixed envelope:
441	
442	```json
443	{
444	  "report": { "exported": 12, "warnings": [] },
445	  "receipt": { "destination": "/tmp/report.csv", "stdout": false, "byte_count": 480 }
446	}
447	```
448	
449	So a template can say what only the framework knows:
450	
451	```jinja
452	Exported {{ report.exported }} rows to {{ receipt.destination }}
453	```
454	
455	The envelope shape is fixed (`report` + `receipt`) whatever the report's type,
456	so no application key can collide with the receipt. Structured modes serialize
457	the same envelope. A failed write renders nothing: success cannot outrun the
458	write that justifies it.
459	
460	#### The report channel
461	
462	Mixing a report into the bytes would corrupt them, so the channel follows the
463	destination:
464	
465	| Artifact destination | Report goes to |
466	| --- | --- |
467	| File | stdout |
468	| Stdout (`allow_stdout()`) | stderr |
469	
470	#### Hooks and artifacts
471	
472	Post-dispatch hooks see the report as ordinary handler data. Post-output hooks
473	see `RenderedOutput::Artifact` and can still transform the bytes or the report
474	via `as_artifact_mut()`. Hooks never perform the write — that stays framework-
475	owned, which is what keeps the failure path single and the report honest.
476	
477	Bytes are owned; streaming is deliberately not part of this contract.
478
